rule: No figure in this ledger is summed or averaged across rows unless a row states the overlap assumption and names the rows it combines.

grades.A: primary official data or model output
grades.C: press, secondary summary, or an organisation's own statement
grades.D: lab judgment, stated as such, with the task that retires it

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, ICD-10 W65–W74. Excludes water transport, flood and other disasters, intentional drowning.
rows.source: WHO Global Health Estimates 2021, summary table (released 2024)
rows.do_not_add_to: Never averaged with ihme-gbd-2021 or who-ghe-2019; never summed with excluded components without stating overlap.
rows.note: Point estimate; the cited table prints no uncertainty interval, which is not the same as no uncertainty. The 2024 report rounds it to 300 000 and gives a global rate of 3.8 per 100 000 (p. 14).

rows.scope: GBD drowning cause; core definition unintentional drowning W65–W74. Same exclusions as WHO.
rows.source: Xie Z et al., Global burden of drowning 1990–2021, Scientific Reports 15:10916 (2025), Table 1
rows.do_not_add_to: Never averaged with who-ghe-2021. The 26,028 gap is model disagreement, not a head count.
rows.note: Independent model and input database from WHO.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, W65–W74; legacy model vintage.
rows.source: WHO Global Health Estimates 2019, summary table (released 2020)
rows.do_not_add_to: Cannot be used with who-ghe-2021 to show a rise 2019→2021: different vintage.
rows.note: Still quoted on some WHO pages.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, W65–W74 / ICD-9 E910.
rows.source: Franklin RC et al., The burden of unintentional drowning, Injury Prevention 26:i83 (2020), GBD 2017
rows.do_not_add_to: Different GBD round from ihme-gbd-2021; do not chain into a trend across rounds.
rows.note: Reports a 44.5% fall since 1990.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, GBD 2017 back-estimate for 1990.
rows.source: Franklin RC et al., Injury Prevention (2020)
rows.do_not_add_to: Trend only within the same GBD round.
rows.note: Basis of the 44.5% decline 1990–2017.

rows.scope: Global drowning death rate, 2000 vs 2021.
rows.source: WHO, Drowning fact sheet (2026)
rows.do_not_add_to: A rate, not a count.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning by World Bank income group.
rows.source: WHO Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 3 (p. 15); confirmed in the report on 15 Oct 2026 (an editorial in Injury Prevention reproduces it as its Table 1)
rows.do_not_add_to: Rows sum to 299,000 because of rounding; a share of who-ghe-2021, not an addition to it.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning by income group.
rows.source: WHO Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 3 (p. 15)

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning by income group.
rows.source: WHO Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 3 (p. 15)
rows.do_not_add_to: Share of the WHO 2021 figure.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning by income group.
rows.source: WHO Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 3 (p. 15)
rows.do_not_add_to: Share of the WHO 2021 figure.

rows.figure: Nearly a quarter of drowning deaths
rows.scope: Children under 5.
rows.source: WHO, Drowning fact sheet
rows.do_not_add_to: A share of one estimate; overlaps with region and income cuts.
rows.note: The 2024 report prints 21% (over 62,000) in some summaries; we chart the fact-sheet wording.

rows.figure: 57% of drowning deaths
rows.scope: Ages 0–29.
rows.source: WHO, Drowning fact sheet
rows.do_not_add_to: Share, not a count.

rows.figure: Male rate more than twice the female rate
rows.scope: Drowning death rate by sex.
rows.source: WHO, Drowning fact sheet
rows.do_not_add_to: Ratio, not a count.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, WHO Western Pacific Region. The report prints deaths to the nearest thousand.
rows.source: WHO, Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 2 (p. 14) and the text on p. 14; figures from WHO Global Health Estimates 2021
rows.do_not_add_to: A share of the WHO global figure; never added to another region's share from a different source.
rows.note: Confirmed 15 Oct 2026 against the report (p. 14: 84 000 deaths, 28% of the global burden). The WHO Western Pacific data page gives the same figure and a rate of 13.7 per 100,000 among people 70 and older.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, WHO South-East Asia Region. The report prints deaths to the nearest thousand.
rows.source: WHO, Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 2 (p. 14) and the text on p. 14; figures from WHO Global Health Estimates 2021
rows.do_not_add_to: A share of the WHO global figure.
rows.note: Upgraded from C to A on 15 Oct 2026 after reading the report: Fig. 2 prints 83 000; p. 14 gives 4.0 per 100 000. WHO fact sheet: over half of the world's drowning occurs in the Western Pacific and South-East Asia Regions.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, WHO African Region. The report prints deaths to the nearest thousand.
rows.source: WHO, Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 2 (p. 14) and the text on p. 14; figures from WHO Global Health Estimates 2021
rows.do_not_add_to: A share of the WHO global figure.
rows.note: Corrected 15 Oct 2026: a secondary summary had given ~77,000 and 5.7; the report's Fig. 2 prints 66 000 and p. 14 gives 5.6 per 100 000, the highest regional rate.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region. The report prints deaths to the nearest thousand.
rows.source: WHO, Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 2 (p. 14) and the text on p. 14; figures from WHO Global Health Estimates 2021
rows.do_not_add_to: A share of the WHO global figure.
rows.note: Corrected 15 Oct 2026 from ~36,000 (secondary summary) to the report's 35 000; rate 4.4 per 100 000 (p. 14). The fact sheet gives this region the highest rate among children under 5: 16.8 per 100,000.

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, WHO Region of the Americas. The report prints deaths to the nearest thousand.
rows.source: WHO, Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 2 (p. 14) and the text on p. 14; figures from WHO Global Health Estimates 2021
rows.do_not_add_to: A share of the WHO global figure.
rows.note: Corrected 15 Oct 2026 from ~16,500 (secondary summary) to the report's 17 000; rate 1.6 per 100 000 (p. 14).

rows.scope: Unintentional drowning, WHO European Region. The report prints deaths to the nearest thousand.
rows.source: WHO, Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, Fig. 2 (p. 14) and the text on p. 14; figures from WHO Global Health Estimates 2021
rows.do_not_add_to: A share of the WHO global figure.
rows.note: Corrected 15 Oct 2026: a secondary summary had given 9,155 and 1.0 per 100,000; the report's Fig. 2 prints 15 000 and p. 14 gives 1.7. The 9,155 figure may come from a different region membership or cause definition; unresolved, and a task on the board.

rows.figure: Drowning death rate down 38% since 2000; deaths down 20%, from 375,000 to 300,000
rows.scope: Global unintentional drowning, 2000 compared with 2021, as the WHO 2024 report states it (p. 17; rates in Fig. 6). Low is 2021, high is 2000.
rows.source: WHO, Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, p. 17 and Fig. 6
rows.do_not_add_to: A trend, not a count to add. The 2000 figure is a back-cast from the same model, not a count made in 2000.
rows.note: By region the rate fell 3% in Africa, 21% in the Eastern Mediterranean, 38% in the Americas, 38% in the Western Pacific, 48% in South-East Asia and 68% in Europe (p. 17). Proposed by an independent agent's bundle on 15 Oct 2026 and read in the report.

rows.figure: 4–5 non-fatal drownings per death (retired: no primary source exists)
rows.scope: A global ratio that appears only in a press article, introduced with "it is estimated", citing the WHO 2024 report, which carries no such ratio.
rows.source: esanum.com, "Drowning: an underestimated global emergency" (press, undated, no byline): the only document found carrying the figure
rows.do_not_add_to: Not deaths. Never added to any death count. Not to be cited as WHO's figure.
rows.note: retired: 2026-10-15. Traced by an independent agent (contributions/nonfatal-ratio-primary-agent-two.json) after reading the WHO 2024 report, the 2014 report, the fact sheet and eleven other documents: no primary states 4–5. Kept so the claim can be traced, not relied on. The counted ratios that exist are place-specific: see ontario-nonfatal-ed-ratio-2014-2023, cdc-nonfatal-ed-2012-2021, australia-nonfatal-hospitalisation-ratio-2002-2015.

rows.figure: Nearly four (3.6) emergency-department visits for non-fatal drowning per water-related death
rows.scope: Ontario emergency-department visits for non-fatal drowning 2014–2023 (about 585 a year, Public Health Ontario from CIHI NACRS) against the average yearly water-related fatalities 2012–2021 (164). Counts only cases that reached an emergency department; the two year windows differ.
rows.source: Lifesaving Society Ontario / Drowning Prevention Research Centre Canada, Ontario Non-Fatal Drowning Report, 2025 edition, pp. 1–2
rows.do_not_add_to: A ratio for one province and one denominator; not global, and never combined with hospital- or ambulance-based ratios.
rows.note: Printed as "nearly four" (pp. 1, 4) and "3.6 times" (p. 2); earlier editions give 3.5–3.6. Found by an independent agent, 15 Oct 2026.

rows.figure: 2.71 hospital separations for non-fatal drowning per fatal drowning (6,158 to 2,272)
rows.scope: Australia, 1 July 2002 to 30 June 2015, all ages. Leaves out emergency-department-only cases and anyone who never reached a hospital. The same paper gives 7.63 for children 0–4 and 4.35 for swimming pools.
rows.source: Peden A.E. et al., Understanding the full burden of drowning, BMJ Open 2018;8(11):e024868
rows.do_not_add_to: A hospitalisation ratio for one country; not an emergency-department ratio, not global.
rows.note: Royal Life Saving Australia rounds it to "three non-fatal for every fatal". Found by an independent agent, 15 Oct 2026.

rows.figure: For every child under 18 who dies from drowning, another 7 receive emergency-department care for non-fatal drowning
rows.scope: United States, children under 18, as stated on a CDC Drowning Facts document last reviewed 7 October 2022. Emergency-department care only.
rows.source: CDC, Drowning Facts (document on CDC Stacks, reviewed 7 Oct 2022)
rows.do_not_add_to: Children only; not to be applied to all ages or to other countries.
rows.note: Children's ratios run far above all-age ratios everywhere they are counted (Australia 0–4: 7.63; New Zealand under 5: 6.9 hospitalisations). Found by an independent agent, 15 Oct 2026.

rows.figure: 178,000 children would avoid severe, life-limiting injuries from non-fatal drowning
rows.scope: WHO's investment-case projection on its drowning fact sheet: the injuries avoided if the recommended measures were scaled up, alongside 774,000 child deaths averted by 2050. A projection, not a count and not a ratio.
rows.source: WHO, Drowning fact sheet (dated 1 May 2026), Prevention section
rows.do_not_add_to: A modelled projection to 2050; never added to any count of events.
rows.note: The only quantified non-fatal figure WHO currently publishes.

rows.figure: About 2 emergency-department visits for non-fatal drowning per death (8,111 visits to 4,083 deaths a year)
rows.scope: United States, 2012–2021 averages: 4,083 unintentional drowning deaths and 8,111 estimated emergency department visits for non-fatal drowning a year. Counts only survivors who reached an emergency department.
rows.source: CDC, Drowning facts (page dated 27 Jan 2026)
rows.do_not_add_to: A US ratio of emergency-department visits to deaths; not a global ratio and not a count of all survivors.
rows.note: The only counted non-fatal ratio in the ledger. Survivors who never reach an emergency department are not in it.

rows.figure: 31% of countries record where a drowning happened; 27% record the activity; 59% record age and sex
rows.scope: Replies from 135 WHO Member States (70%) and four territories to the report's questionnaire, on what their drowning data record.
rows.source: WHO Global status report on drowning prevention 2024, executive summary (p. x) and p. 7
rows.do_not_add_to: A survey result, not a count.
rows.note: Upgraded from C to A on 15 Oct 2026 by reading the report: place of drowning collected by 31% of countries, activity by 27%, age and sex by 59%; 26% report a national strategy specific to drowning (p. 33). This is the gap the register pilot is written for.

rows.figure: Drowning is 75% of deaths in flood disasters
rows.scope: Share of flood-disaster deaths that are drownings.
rows.source: WHO, Drowning fact sheet
rows.do_not_add_to: A share, not a count. Applied to a flood-death count it gives an estimate, not an observation.

rows.figure: 5,110 flood deaths
rows.scope: Deaths attributed to flood disasters, all causes.
rows.source: CRED, Natural disasters 2019 (EM-DAT)
rows.do_not_add_to: All causes, not only drowning. Yearly totals swing several-fold.
rows.note: With who-flood-share: about 3,800 flood drownings in 2019.

rows.figure: ~3,000–8,000 flood drownings a year
rows.scope: Lab band: 75% of EM-DAT flood deaths, allowing for year-to-year swings.
rows.source: Lab judgment from who-flood-share and EM-DAT yearly totals
rows.do_not_add_to: A band we drew. Replace it with a sourced multi-year average and this row is retired.
rows.note: Open task: compute 75% of EM-DAT flood deaths for 2010–2024.

rows.figure: 800–1,000 ferry deaths a year; could be twice that
rows.scope: Deaths in ferry accidents worldwide.
rows.source: Worldwide Ferry Safety Association (R. Weisbrod), quoted in Foreign Policy, 16 Apr 2014
rows.do_not_add_to: Ferries only; other shipping and small craft have no global series. Outside the WHO figure by definition.
rows.note: Old estimate. Open task: ask WFSA for its current database totals.

rows.figure: No global yearly series
rows.scope: Shipping, small craft capsize, work boats, not counted as ferries.
rows.source: None found
rows.do_not_add_to: Cannot be drawn. Single disasters sit in the ledger when sourced.
rows.note: The largest unmeasured piece of the toll.

rows.figure: 24,000 fishing deaths a year
rows.scope: Occupational deaths in fishing.
rows.source: ILO (1999), from the FAO 1987 proposal
rows.do_not_add_to: How much falls inside the WHO figure is unresolved; do not add without stating an overlap assumption.
rows.note: Still used by authorities; called "seemingly faulty, decades-old" by FISH Safety Foundation.

rows.figure: More than 32,000 a year
rows.scope: Occupational deaths in fishing, as quoted by WHO.
rows.source: FAO, quoted in the WHO drowning fact sheet
rows.do_not_add_to: Overlap with the WHO figure unresolved.

rows.figure: More than 100,000 a year
rows.scope: Occupational deaths in fishing, all causes.
rows.source: FISH Safety Foundation; Willis S, Holliday E et al., Marine Policy (2023)
rows.do_not_add_to: Not all drownings; overlap with the WHO figure unresolved.
rows.note: No comprehensive global data on fisher deaths exists; no agreed definition of a fisher.

rows.figure: 9,191 dead or missing on migration routes
rows.scope: All routes, land and sea.
rows.source: IOM Missing Migrants Project, as reported to the UN (2025)
rows.do_not_add_to: Not all at sea; not all drownings. Excluded from the WHO figure.
rows.note: Deadliest year on record at the time.

rows.figure: At least 3,650 died on maritime migration journeys
rows.scope: Sea routes worldwide, Sept 2024–May 2025.
rows.source: IOM Missing Migrants Project (UN submission, June 2025)
rows.do_not_add_to: A minimum; two-thirds of Mediterranean dead remain missing.
rows.note: Over 1,600 drowned in the Mediterranean in this window.

rows.figure: ~4,200 on three sea routes, plus ~1,500 estimated in unrecorded wrecks
rows.scope: Mediterranean 2,185; Atlantic route to the Canaries 1,214; Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea 800+.
rows.source: IOM 2025 figures as reported by press (Diplomatic Insight, Jan 2026)
rows.do_not_add_to: A minimum for three routes only. Verify against IOM's own 2025 release.
rows.note: IOM warns that a lower total does not mean lower risk: verification and access limits affect the count.

rows.figure: 39,383 drowned during unsafe migration since 2014
rows.scope: Cumulative, 2014 to Dec 2024.
rows.source: IOM Missing Migrants Project, quoted by WHO (Dec 2024)
rows.do_not_add_to: Cumulative over a decade; never a yearly figure. WHO states these are excluded from its global estimates.

rows.figure: No global series reproduced
rows.scope: Intentional and undetermined-intent drowning (ICD X71, Y21).
rows.source: None reproduced in this pass
rows.do_not_add_to: Outside the unintentional core by definition. A different problem with different prevention.
rows.note: Open task: reproduce GBD self-harm by drowning from a primary table.

rows.figure: 4,345 unintentional drowning deaths a year, average
rows.scope: Average 2018–2021.
rows.source: CDC, Drowning data (27 Jan 2026)
rows.do_not_add_to: Windows overlap with us-cdc-4500; never averaged.

rows.figure: Over 4,500 drowned each year
rows.scope: Average 2020–2022.
rows.source: CDC Vital Signs (18 Jun 2024); MMWR (14 May 2024)
rows.do_not_add_to: Overlaps us-cdc-4345.

rows.figure: 556 recreational boating deaths; 3 in 4 drowned; 87% of those wore no life jacket
rows.scope: Recreational boating fatalities.
rows.source: U.S. Coast Guard, 2024 Recreational Boating Statistics
rows.do_not_add_to: A subset of US drownings plus non-drowning boating deaths; not added to CDC figures.
rows.note: About 70% of deaths involved an operator with no boating safety instruction; alcohol the leading known factor (20%). Fewest deaths in 50+ years.

rows.figure: 14,282 SAR cases; 5,892 lives saved
rows.scope: Search and rescue, fiscal year 2024.
rows.source: U.S. Coast Guard Office of Search and Rescue
rows.do_not_add_to: "Lives saved" uses the Coast Guard's own definition.

rows.figure: 348 US drowning deaths a year preventable by pool fencing and life jackets
rows.scope: Modeled: isolation pool fencing for under-5s and always wearing a life jacket while boating.
rows.source: Peterson C et al., Injury Prevention (2025), doi:10.1136/ip-2024-045597
rows.do_not_add_to: A model, not a count.
rows.note: The $4.5 billion in the paper is the yearly economic cost of those deaths, not the cost of fences or jackets.

rows.figure: 774,000 fewer child drownings by 2050
rows.scope: Modeled: day-care for pre-school children plus basic swim skills.
rows.source: WHO, Hidden depths: the global investment case for drowning prevention (2023)
rows.do_not_add_to: A projection to 2050, never a yearly share of 300,000.
rows.note: Return estimated at 9 times the cost.

rows.figure: Six recommended measures
rows.scope: Control access to water; day-care for pre-school children; swim, water-safety and safe-rescue skills; safe boating, shipping and ferry rules; flood preparedness; a national water safety strategy.
rows.source: WHO, Drowning fact sheet, Prevention
rows.do_not_add_to: Recommendations, not counts.

rows.figure: No published global share of preventable drowning deaths
rows.scope: Checked 12 Oct 2026.
rows.source: None found
rows.do_not_add_to: We will not draw one.

rows.figure: Exclusions "almost halve" drowning figures in high-income contexts like Australia
rows.scope: Effect of excluding water transport and disasters from the core definition.
rows.source: Injury Prevention editorial on the WHO 2024 report, PMC12911604
rows.do_not_add_to: A statement about definitions, not a global multiplier.
rows.note: Evidence that the true toll sits above the core in some settings.

rows.figure: Core = ICD-10 W65–W74; excluded X38, V90, V92, Y21
rows.scope: What the core drowning estimates include and leave out.
rows.source: Özanne-Smith J et al., PLOS ONE (2022), PMC9341097
rows.do_not_add_to: A definition.
rows.note: X38 flood, V90/V92 water transport, Y21 undetermined intent.

rows.figure: 147,096 lives saved since 1824
rows.scope: RNLI cumulative, by its published definition.
rows.source: RNLI annual accounts 2025
rows.do_not_add_to: Cumulative; a definition the RNLI publishes.

rows.figure: "Hundreds" of lives in ~70 rescues · 60+ major rescues · 1,678 seafarers aided 1918–1939
rows.scope: Three counts from three sources about one station.
rows.source: EPA; Maine Preservation (2026); Down East (2022), from station records
rows.do_not_add_to: Three counts that are not a total. Aided is not saved.

rows.figure: Over 4 knots on the ebb (maximum average velocity, off Nobles Island and off Dover Point)
rows.scope: Maximum average tidal current velocity in the Piscataqua River. Deep-draft navigation is limited to 1.5 hours either side of slack water; strong currents and eddies in the bend at Fort Point.
rows.source: NOAA, U.S. Coast Pilot 1, Chapter 9 (20 Sep 2026 edition), paragraphs 296, 369 and 371
rows.do_not_add_to: A current speed, not a count. It is the maximum average; the river is slower near slack and in the coves.
rows.note: Upgraded 15 Oct 2026 from a lab statement (grade D) to the NOAA Coast Pilot. A kayak paddles about three knots; a swimmer far less.

rows.figure: Mean monthly sea temperature 2.9 °C (March) to 16.7 °C (August); June mean 12.5 °C
rows.scope: Climatic summary of NOAA buoy 44007, 12 nautical miles southeast of Portland, Maine, February 1982 to December 2008; monthly means with extremes.
rows.geography: Gulf of Maine, off Portland ME
rows.source: NOAA National Data Buoy Center, station 44007 climatic summary
rows.do_not_add_to: A temperature, not a count. The buoy is about 50 nautical miles up the coast from Portsmouth; harbor and river water differ from the open gulf.
rows.note: In June, when the lab runs, the sea is about 12 °C (54 °F). Cold-water immersion rules apply here all year.

rows.figure: Leeway: the movement of a craft through the water caused by the wind acting on its exposed surface
rows.scope: The U.S. National SAR Manual's definition, as quoted by the Coast Guard R&D Center's review of leeway field experiments (Section 1.3, p. 1-2). The review's recommended values by object class (Table 8-1) are a task on the board.
rows.source: Allen A.A. & Plourde J.V., Review of Leeway: Field Experiments and Implementation, USCG R&D Center report CG-D-08-99 (April 1999)
rows.do_not_add_to: A definition, not a figure.
rows.note: The quantity a drift worksheet needs, object by object, before a search area can be drawn. Recommended values not yet transcribed: see the board.

rows.figure: Measured surface currents 6× more accurate than modelled; search area reduced by about two-thirds
rows.scope: HF radar surface currents feeding search planning.
rows.source: Rutgers RUCOOL, 20th-anniversary HF radar SAR presentation (2024), citing Roarty et al. 2018
rows.do_not_add_to: A technical claim, not a count of lives.
rows.note: Relevant to the Drift pilot track.

rows.figure: Fishing-vessel safety treaty enters into force 24 Feb 2027, for vessels of 24 m and over
rows.scope: IMO Cape Town Agreement of 2012; 28 states acceded by Feb 2026.
rows.source: IMO press briefing; DNV statutory news (2026)
rows.do_not_add_to: A milestone, not a count. Boats under 24 m, where most fishing deaths happen, are outside it.

rows.figure: Chance of drowning at a USLA-guarded beach: 1 in 18 million
rows.scope: Fatal drowning at beaches protected by USLA-affiliated lifeguards, from ten years of agency reports.
rows.source: United States Lifesaving Association, Statistics
rows.do_not_add_to: An organisation's own calculation; the denominator is beach attendance as agencies report it.
rows.note: Strong practice evidence for guarded swim areas; not a controlled study.

rows.figure: Life jacket wear: adjusted risk ratio 0.51 (95% CI 0.35–0.74) for drowning among recreational boaters
rows.scope: US Coast Guard boating data 2000–2006, matched cohort.
rows.source: Cummings P, Mueller BA, Quan L. Injury Prevention 17:156 (2011)
rows.do_not_add_to: A ratio, not a count. The authors caution the estimate may be biased because many vessels were excluded.
rows.note: If the association is causal, wearing a life jacket may prevent one in two boating drownings.

rows.figure: Pool fencing: OR 0.27 (0.16–0.47) vs no fence; four-sided isolation fencing OR 0.17 (0.07–0.44) vs three-sided
rows.scope: Drowning and near-drowning in young children; three case-control studies. Searches last updated Oct 2006.
rows.source: Thompson DC, Rivara FP. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD001047
rows.do_not_add_to: Ratios, not counts.
rows.note: The clearest evidence in the tree: a fence that separates the pool from the house.

rows.figure: 1 minute to control breathing · 10 minutes of useful movement · about 1 hour before hypothermia takes consciousness
rows.scope: Cold-water immersion phases, from laboratory and field work with volunteers.
rows.source: Gordon Giesbrecht, University of Manitoba (the 1-10-1 principle), as explained by McGill OSS
rows.do_not_add_to: A teaching rule, not a count, and never a reason to delay a call.
rows.note: The clock pilot track turns this into a hand-size card and tests whether crews use it.

rows.figure: Village crèches: 82% fewer child drowning deaths (RR 0.181); SwimSafe lessons: 93% fewer (RR 0.072)
rows.scope: Children in rural Bangladesh, 2006–2010, versus matched non-participants. Cost per DALY averted: crèches $812, SwimSafe $85.
rows.source: Rahman F, Bose S, Linnan M et al. Pediatrics 130(6):e1621 (2012)
rows.do_not_add_to: Ratios from one country programme; not a global share.
rows.note: The evidence behind WHO's day-care and swim-skills recommendations and its 2050 investment case.

rows.figure: 357 drowning deaths
rows.scope: 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025, all drowning deaths as the report defines them.
rows.source: Royal Life Saving Society Australia, National Drowning Report 2025
rows.do_not_add_to: A national count with its own definition; not comparable to UK or US rows without that definition.

rows.figure: Coastal 154 (43%) · inland waterways 122 (34%) · swimming pools 35 (10%); rivers and creeks 99, beaches 82
rows.scope: Drowning deaths by location, Australia, July 2024–June 2025. Inland = rivers, creeks, lakes and dams. 68% of pool deaths were in backyard pools.
rows.source: Royal Life Saving Society Australia, National Drowning Report 2025 (news summary, 26 Aug 2025)
rows.do_not_add_to: Shares of one national count; the categories do not sum to 357 because some locations are not listed.
rows.note: A real split by water setting, for one country that counts. The first entry toward gap 4.

rows.figure: 65 and older: 118 (33%) · 15–24: 44, up 38% on the ten-year average · under 5: 15, down 21%
rows.scope: Drowning deaths by age, Australia, July 2024–June 2025. The report says people 75 and older have the highest rates.
rows.source: Royal Life Saving Society Australia, National Drowning Report 2025 (news summary)
rows.do_not_add_to: Shares of one national count.
rows.note: In a high-income country the age profile inverts: older adults, not under-fives, carry the largest share.

rows.figure: No measure of how many people are on the water
rows.scope: Rates are published per 100,000 residents, not per hour or per trip on the water. Risk per trip is unknown everywhere.
rows.source: None found
rows.do_not_add_to: Cannot be drawn. Without it, no rate on this site is a risk.
rows.note: Open task: count launches at one ramp for one season; pair with AIS for larger vessels.

rows.figure: Event-level records of every reported US recreational boating accident
rows.scope: Boating Accident Report Database: vessel, activity, weather, life-jacket use, outcome, per accident.
rows.source: U.S. Coast Guard, Boating Accident Report Database (BARD) and annual statistics
rows.do_not_add_to: US boating only; reporting thresholds apply.
rows.note: Proof that event-level records with activity and life-jacket fields can be kept at national scale.

rows.figure: 193 accidental water-related deaths; 84% male; 61% inland
rows.scope: Accidental water-related fatalities, UK, with 206 cases of unknown cause still open with coroners.
rows.source: National Water Safety Forum, Water Incident Database (WAID) 2024
rows.do_not_add_to: Accidental only; the open coroner cases may add to it. Not comparable to other countries without the definition.
